So I built a prototype where this takes one gesture Oleg Sadovyi 5 min read · Sep 30, 2026 -- Listen Share For a long time I have wanted to easily sort products into wishlists. And every time I ran into the same thing: technically the feature exists almost everywhere, but actually using it is uncomfortable. Take Zalando. They have one of the best wishlist implementations on the market, with proper boards. But to put an item into a specific board, you have to click the heart, wait for a popup, pick a list and confirm. Every time. On every single product. So I built a prototype where this takes one gesture. Here is what came out of it, and honestly — where it breaks. Desktop: olegsadovyi.github.io/favorites.html Mobile: olegsadovyi.github.io/favorites-mobile.html Press enter or click to view image in full size The problem To put a product into the right list today, you have to perform four actions instead of one. Press enter or click to view image in full size Click the heart. Wait for the popup. Choose a list. Confirm. And here is an important nuance. The popup is not a design mistake. It is a correct solution to a real problem: the system does not know which list you want, so it has to ask. The issue is that this price gets charged every single time. Even when I know exactly where the item goes. Even on the tenth product in a row. The result is predictable. At some point people stop choosing and just tap the heart. Everything lands in the default list. Six months later there are a hundred items sitting in one pile, and the wishlist has turned into a junk drawer. Which means the saving interface decides whether sorting happens at all. Nobody goes back to organize their wishlist afterwards. If it did not happen at the moment of saving, it will never happen. What the prototype does You drag a product straight into the list you want. The lists stay visible on screen while you drag — in the prototype they are “List jeans”, “List for party” and “List for work”. Press enter or click to view image in full size On mobile it is a long press on the product, then a drag to the Favourites tab on the right edge of the screen. Press enter or click to view image in full size There is Undo and Reset to roll an action back. What works One gesture instead of a chain. Intent and destination are expressed in a single movement. The system does not ask “where to?” because the answer is already inside the action. No modal. The catalog is not covered, the browsing context is not destroyed. The person does not drop out of the “I am looking at products” state — and that state is exactly what usually gets broken. You see the destination while you act. No need to remember what you named your lists two months ago. They are right there. Sorting happens at the moment of saving. This is the main one. Not later, not someday — right now, while the context is still in your head. What does not work Being honest here, because these are serious. It is an invisible mechanic. Nothing tells you that a product can be dragged at all. You need a hint — and hints come with their own price. I have already dealt with a case where a tutorial popup lifted feature usage and cut overall conversion at the same time. It is easy to replace one popup with another. The gesture is precise and slow. A long press plus a drag on mobile takes longer than a simple tap on a heart. For people with motor impairments it is a real barrier. Drag and drop without an alternative path means the feature becomes unavailable to part of your audience. It does not scale with the number of lists. Three lists fit on a screen. Fifteen do not. After that you need scrolling while dragging, which is one of the worst interactions that exist. The popup does not go away. Creating a new list still has to live somewhere. So drag and drop does not replace the old path, it sits on top of it. That is not a simpler interface — it is one more layer. Accidental drops. Which is why Undo in the prototype is not decoration. It is mandatory. Conclusion: who this actually works for My conclusion is this: drag and drop is not a replacement for the popup. It is a fast lane on top of it. It works for people who save a lot and keep several lists. Call it 10–20% of the base, generating most of the saves — and exactly the group that a flat wishlist hurts the most. For them, saving four steps on every product is something you feel physically. It does not work for someone who saves two items a year. They have nothing to sort, they will never learn the gesture, and the popup suits them fine. So the logic is: the heart plus popup stays the default for everyone, and drag and drop switches on as an accelerator once a person has more than one list. The mechanic appears when it starts to make sense. And the metric here is not “how many people dragged a product”. The metric is what share of saves land in a named list instead of the default pile. If that share grows, the interface works. If it does not, we just added another way to do the same thing. Go poke the prototype — curious to hear what feels awkward.
